The quiet hum of the city at night is a symphony of forgotten stories. Streetlights flicker like distant lanterns, casting long shadows over pavement that whispers secrets of a thousand hands. A pigeon, unperturbed, pecks at crumbs from a discarded sandwich, its feathers ruffled by the breeze that carries the scent of rain and old books from a nearby library. The air smells like the last remnants of a summer’s heat, mixed with the cool tang of pavement after a drizzle.

I sit on a bench, my fingers tracing the edge of a half-empty coffee cup. The city breathes around me—cars passing in the distance, the occasional laugh from a group of strangers, the distant wail of a siren. It’s all so ordinary, yet so vivid. Life here is a tapestry of routines, but beneath the surface, there’s something wild. A child’s laughter cutting through the noise, a stray dog darting between parked cars, a musician playing a forgotten tune on a corner stool.

Sometimes, I wonder if the city remembers. Does it hold onto the faces of those who once lived here, or does it just keep moving forward, indifferent? The buildings stand tall, their windows like eyes watching over the chaos. They’ve seen love stories end, dreams take flight, and people disappear into the night. The city doesn’t judge; it just endures.

I close my eyes and imagine a time when the streets were quieter, when people walked slower, when the world felt smaller. Maybe then, the noise wouldn’t feel so overwhelming. Maybe then, I’d remember to breathe.
